vjimc-1995-cat2-01.title: Gradients are perpendicular
vjimc-1995-cat2-01.body:
Let $F(x,y)=x^2-y^2$ and $G(x,y)=xy$. The curves (1) and (2) are level sets $F=a$ and $G=b$.

The gradients are
$$
abla F=(2x,-2y),\qquad 
abla G=(y,x).$$
Both vanish only at the origin. The origin lies on curve (1) only when $a=0$ and on curve (2) only when $b=0$; these are the degenerate "hyperbolas" (pairs of lines $y=\pm x$ and the coordinate axes), so we take $a
e0$ or $b
e0$. Then at any intersection point $P=(x,y)
e(0,0)$ both gradients are nonzero, and the curves are smooth there with tangent lines perpendicular to $
abla F(P)$ and $
abla G(P)$ respectively.

Since
$$
abla F\cdot
abla G=2xy-2xy=0,$$
the normals at $P$ are perpendicular, hence so are the tangents. So every hyperbola of family (1) meets every hyperbola of family (2) at a right angle, i.e. the two systems are orthogonal. ∎

vjimc-1995-cat2-01.title: Conformal map $z\mapsto z^2$
vjimc-1995-cat2-01.body:
Write $z=x+iy$. Then $w=z^2=(x^2-y^2)+2ixy$. The curve (1) is the preimage of the vertical line $\operatorname{Re}w=a$, and the curve (2) is the preimage of the horizontal line $\operatorname{Im}w=2b$.

The map $z\mapsto z^2$ is holomorphic with derivative $2z
e0$ for $z
e0$, so it is conformal (angle-preserving) away from the origin. The images of the two curves, a vertical and a horizontal line, meet at a right angle. So at every intersection point $z_0
e0$ the curves (1) and (2) also meet at a right angle. ∎

vjimc-1995-cat2-02.title: Pair symmetric terms and use $z^m+z^{-m}$ as a polynomial in $z+z^{-1}$
vjimc-1995-cat2-02.body:
We assume, as intended, that $f$ has degree $2n$, i.e. $f_{2n}=f_0\ne0$. (Otherwise the same argument gives $\deg g\le n$.) Put $w=z+z^{-1}$.

**Lemma.** For every $m\ge0$ there is a polynomial $P_m$ with $z^m+z^{-m}=P_m(w)$ for all $z\ne0$. Moreover $P_0=2$, and for $m\ge1$, $P_m$ is monic of degree $m$.

*Proof.* $P_0=2$ and $P_1(w)=w$. For $m\ge1$,
$$(z+z^{-1})(z^m+z^{-m})=z^{m+1}+z^{-(m+1)}+z^{m-1}+z^{-(m-1)},$$
so $P_{m+1}(w)=wP_m(w)-P_{m-1}(w)$. By induction $P_{m+1}$ is a polynomial, and it is monic of degree $m+1$ because $wP_m$ is monic of degree $m+1$ while $P_{m-1}$ has degree $m-1$. $\square$

**Main argument.** For $z\ne0$,
$$z^{-n}f(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{2n}f_kz^{k-n}=f_n+\sum_{m=1}^{n}\left(f_{n+m}z^{m}+f_{n-m}z^{-m}\right).$$
By hypothesis $f_{n-m}=f_{2n-(n-m)}=f_{n+m}$, so
$$z^{-n}f(z)=f_n+\sum_{m=1}^n f_{n+m}\left(z^m+z^{-m}\right)=f_n+\sum_{m=1}^n f_{n+m}P_m(w).$$
Define
$$g(w)=f_n+\sum_{m=1}^n f_{n+m}P_m(w).$$
This is a polynomial. Its only term of degree $n$ comes from $m=n$, with coefficient $f_{2n}\ne0$ (each $P_m$ is monic of degree $m$). So $\deg g=n$, and $f(z)=z^ng(z+z^{-1})$ for all $z\ne0$, which is the claimed identity. ∎

vjimc-1995-cat2-03.title: Use $\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$
vjimc-1995-cat2-03.body:
Yes. Put
$$g(x)=f(x)\sin x,\qquad h(x)=f(x)\cos x .$$
These are products of continuous functions, hence continuous on $\mathbb R$, and for every $x$
$$g(x)\sin x+h(x)\cos x=f(x)\left(\sin^2x+\cos^2x\right)=f(x).$$

**Answer: Yes.** ∎

vjimc-1995-cat2-04.title: Monotone and bounded
vjimc-1995-cat2-04.body:
**Claim.** $0<\arctan x<x$ for every $x>0$.

Indeed, $\arctan x>0$ for $x>0$. Let $h(x)=x-\arctan x$. Then $h(0)=0$ and $h'(x)=1-\frac1{1+x^2}=\frac{x^2}{1+x^2}>0$ for $x\ne0$, so $h(x)>0$ for $x>0$.

Since $x_1=25>0$, induction with the claim gives $0<x_{n}=\arctan x_{n-1}<x_{n-1}$ for all $n\ge2$. So $(x_n)$ is strictly decreasing and bounded below by $0$, hence it converges to some $L\ge0$.

Because $\arctan$ is continuous, letting $n\to\infty$ in $x_n=\arctan x_{n-1}$ gives $L=\arctan L$. If $L>0$, the claim gives $\arctan L<L$, a contradiction. Hence $L=0$.

**Answer: $\lim_{n\to\infty}x_n=0$.** ∎
